questions.question: A PRG stretches a 128-bit seed to 10,000 bits. What is the security level of the output?
options: 128 bits — stretching does not add security, only the seed length matters
10,000 bits — the output is longer so it is more secure
It depends on the hash function used for stretching
0 bits — a PRG is never secure
questions.explanation: PRG security = seed security. An adversary only needs to guess the 128-bit seed to reproduce all 10,000 output bits. The stretch adds length but not entropy.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a PRF and a PRP?
options: A PRP is bijective (invertible) for each key; a PRF has no injectivity requirement
A PRF uses a shorter key than a PRP
A PRP can only be applied to fixed-length inputs; a PRF cannot
A PRF is faster than a PRP for the same security level
questions.explanation: PRP: bijection (permutation) — no two distinct inputs produce the same output. PRF: no such constraint. AES is a PRP; HMAC is a PRF. The PRP-PRF switching lemma bounds how different they are.

questions.question: AES-128 has a 128-bit block size. After how many AES encryptions does the PRP-PRF switching advantage exceed 2^{-32}?
options: About 2^48 — from q*(q-1)/(2*2^128) ≤ 2^{-32}, solving gives q ≈ 2^48.5
Exactly 2^64 — always safe up to the birthday bound
2^32 — the block size divided by 4
2^128 — AES-128 is secure up to its full key space
questions.explanation: From q²/2^{129} ≤ 2^{-32}: q ≤ sqrt(2^{97}) ≈ 2^{48.5}. NIST recommends 2^{48} as the practical limit for a single AES-128 key in CBC/CTR mode.

questions.question: Why does nonce reuse in CTR mode completely break confidentiality?
options: Both messages are XORed with the same keystream, so XOR-ing the two ciphertexts gives plaintext1 XOR plaintext2
The nonce is transmitted in the clear, so the adversary knows the key
CTR mode requires unique nonces only for authentication, not confidentiality
The PRF outputs repeat when the nonce is reused, creating a detectable pattern
questions.explanation: CTR keystream = PRF(k, nonce||i). Same nonce → same keystream. ct1 = m1 XOR ks, ct2 = m2 XOR ks. ct1 XOR ct2 = m1 XOR m2. Any knowledge of m1 reveals m2 completely.

questions.question: Why was the Sweet32 attack possible against 3DES and Blowfish?
options: Both use 64-bit blocks. After 2^32 encryptions, the birthday bound gives ~50% probability of a block collision, breaking security
Their key sizes are too short for modern standards
They use a weak round function that can be distinguished from a PRF
64-bit blocks make decryption faster than encryption, enabling attacks
questions.explanation: PRP-PRF switching: Adv ≤ q²/2^{n+1}. For n=64: Adv = 0.5 at q = 2^32 ≈ 4 billion blocks. At typical network speeds this is reached in hours. Sweet32 exploited birthday collisions in CBC mode with 64-bit blocks.

questions.question: How is a PRG constructed from a PRF (counter-mode construction)?
options: G(k) = F(k, 0) || F(k, 1) || F(k, 2) || … (concatenate PRF outputs for successive counters)
G(k) = F(k, k) (evaluate the PRF on itself)
G(k) = F(k, random) for a fresh random input
G(k) = F(k, 0) XOR F(k, 1) (XOR two PRF calls)
questions.explanation: Counter-mode PRG: extend the seed using the PRF in counter mode. Each F(k, i) produces one block of pseudorandom output. Security follows from PRF security: if F is secure, an adversary cannot distinguish the concatenated outputs from uniform.

questions.question: CTR mode achieves IND-CPA security. What exactly does IND-CPA guarantee?
options: No PPT adversary can distinguish encryptions of two chosen plaintexts of equal length, even after making polynomially many encryption queries
The scheme is secure against chosen-ciphertext attacks
The scheme is information-theoretically secure
The adversary cannot decrypt any ciphertext it did not produce
questions.explanation: IND-CPA (indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack): the adversary picks m0, m1, receives enc(m_b) for random b, and wins if it guesses b with non-negligible advantage. CTR achieves this assuming the PRF is secure — but it does NOT prevent ciphertext tampering (requires IND-CCA or authentication).

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the PRG → PRF → PRP derivation chain?
options: PRG can build PRF via GGM tree; PRF can build PRP via Feistel networks (Luby-Rackoff); OWF can build PRG
PRF implies PRG implies PRP, so a PRP is strictly stronger than a PRG
AES is proven to be a PRG, which implies it is also a PRF and PRP
PRG, PRF, and PRP are independent assumptions with no known implications between them
questions.explanation: The known hierarchy: OWF → PRG (Håstad-Impagliazzo-Levin-Luby), PRG → PRF (GGM tree), PRF → PRP (Feistel, Luby-Rackoff). In practice AES is directly assumed to be a PRP; the theoretical derivation is important for foundations but not for applied usage.
